summary:
Consensual sexual acts between adults are legal in Benin. Article 545 of the Penal Code, in force since 2018, sets an equal age of consent regardless of sex, while keeping heavier penalties for an indecent or unnatural act with a minor of the same sex. Legality is not the same as protection: the general indecency provision has been used to prosecute same-sex conduct, and no criminal ruling on the same-sex provisions had ever been rendered as of Benin's statement to the 2008 review, on the government's account because families would not allow children to be brought to court.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics, and there is no protection on grounds of gender identity at all. Legal gender recognition is impossible. A trans visitor has no recognition pathway to rely on and no statutory protection against discrimination in employment, services, or public life.

Service denial is documented and specific. LGBTQI+ persons are routinely refused medical care, including hormone treatment, as well as social services; healthcare providers regularly refuse gender-affirming hormone therapy and also deny general care such as malaria treatment. Employers often will not hire people known to be LGBTQ, with transgender and intersex people singled out. The US State Department's 2023 report records hostility toward the community especially outside major urban areas, an urban/rural split a visitor should weigh.

Violence risk is real and largely unpunished. Anti-gay lynchings are described as commonplace in Benin in an April 2024 report; violence and lynchings are mostly committed by civilians rather than state authorities, and police rarely pursue perpetrators. Those who report violence or discrimination to police conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity out of fear of mistreatment. The most recent documented public event in this record is a 17 May 2013 International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia gathering in Cotonou drawing 200 people; no later incident is documented here.

Small survivor-support infrastructure exists. The Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre has housed LGBT+ youth since about 2020, a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed; a separate account describes 20 shelters run between 2020 and 2024 housing 380 LGBTQ people. These are the only documented support structures in this inventory.

Religion is a significant source of hostility. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries, priests are documented calling transgender people demons, and imams, priests and traditional healers perform conversion therapy often coerced by families. Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques participate in homophobic preaching. A 2015 account describes LGBT Catholics in Benin, Ghana, Togo and Nigeria facing discrimination from both churches and governments; that account is dated 2015 and is context rather than current-state evidence.

Same-sex couples and families are not recognised by the government, though it grants diplomatic visas and immunity to same-sex partners of foreign diplomats. Article 104(d) of the Children's Code (Law 2015-08) bars foreign homosexual couples from international adoption. Limited protections exist on paper: Article 394 of the Digital Code (Law 2017-20) prohibits processing personal data revealing sex life or sexual orientation, Article 6 of the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law prohibits collection without consent, Article 23 of Law 2011-26 requires business leaders to prevent sexual harassment, and Article 552 of Law 2017-20 punishes incitement to discrimination or hatred on grounds of sexual orientation by electronic network with one year imprisonment and a five million CFA francs fine, in force since 2018. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Benin rejected states' recommendations to improve the situation for LGBTQ persons in the 2012 Universal Periodic Review, with a 4 March 2013 meeting noting that certain things would be rectified. Of fifteen 2023 UPR recommendations, the government accepted two: one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people, and one to combat stigma against HIV. Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restrictions for LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
Historical baseline: anthropologist Patrick Awondo cites evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin, and Melville Herskovits recorded women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom, now Benin, framing same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import. Today's statutory legality therefore rests on pre-colonial practice, not recent liberalisation.

Public events are permitted: LGBTQ associations held a public International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia event at the Institut Francais in Cotonou on 17 May 2013, drawing 200 people. Homosexuality is nonetheless widely perceived as unnatural and as a disease brought by white people, with homosexuals considered deviants.

Benin's Penal Code history includes draft provisions never enacted: Article 88 of the 1996 draft would have punished same-sex acts with one to three years imprisonment and a 100,000 to 500,000 francs fine but was never voted into law, and the October 2008 draft includes no punishment for same-sex relations between consenting adults in private and has not been voted on. The prior Article 331 of the old Penal Code and a 1947 amendment punished an indecent act with a minor of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years imprisonment and a fine of 200 to 50,000 francs.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether Benin's Penal Code or other statutes contain any provision addressing gender identity or trans status directly; the only trans-specific findings are societal, namely priests documented calling transgender people demons and hiring discrimination singling out transgender and intersex people. No legal gender recognition procedure of any kind is documented.

The claim that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace rests on a single April 2024 source's framing; the inventory provides no count, period, or denominator for those incidents, and no per-capita comparison to Benin's general homicide rate. The magnitude of violence risk is therefore unresolved in this record.

Whether the Hirondelles Club figures of almost 380 young people since about 2020 and 20 shelters housing 380 people between 2020 and 2024 describe the same programme is not resolved; the two accounts may be counting the same or different efforts.

The 2015 Washington Blade account of LGBT Catholics facing church and government discrimination is dated 2015 and is treated here as context, not current-state evidence. No later source in this inventory documents religious-institution treatment of trans people specifically.

No source in this inventory addresses airport screening, document markers at Benin's borders, or entry procedures specific to trans travellers; those questions are not sourced here.
